1	\section{Results}
2	\label{sec:results}
3	
4	\subsection{Count-Degradation Curves}
5	\label{sec:count_curves}
6	
7	We first examine how extraction performance changes as the number of types in the prompt schema increases (Experiment~1). Figure~\ref{fig:count_curves} plots per-task metrics across count levels.
8	
9	\paragraph{NER (Few-NERD).}
10	Recall declines monotonically from 0.72 at count${}\,=\,1$ to 0.42 at count${}\,=\,64$, a 42\% relative drop. Precision moves in the opposite direction, rising from 0.11 to 0.52, reflecting a shift from over-prediction to under-prediction as more candidate types compete in the prompt. F1 exhibits an inverted-U shape, peaking at intermediate counts where the precision--recall trade-off is most balanced.
11	
12	\paragraph{RE (FewRel).}
13	Accuracy drops monotonically from 85.7\% at count${}\,=\,1$ to 50.4\% at count${}\,=\,80$, a near-halving when the model must discriminate among all 80 relation types simultaneously.
14	
15	\paragraph{ED (MAVEN).}
16	In contrast to NER and RE, MAVEN relaxed F1 \emph{increases} from 0.106 at count${}\,=\,1$ to 0.247 at count${}\,=\,44$. This reversal arises from three properties of the MAVEN setup: (i)~trigger-level relaxed matching, which requires only token overlap rather than exact span match; (ii)~MAVEN's 168 event types derive from the FrameNet ontology, forming a same-domain hierarchy where co-presented types provide disambiguating context; and (iii)~extreme class imbalance---rare event types benefit from being presented alongside related types that prime the model toward the correct semantic region. We return to this mechanism in \S\ref{sec:centrality_confound}.
17	
18	\paragraph{Summary.}
19	Schema size degrades extraction quality for NER and RE (Channel~1: count $\to$ recall decline), but this pattern does not hold universally. MAVEN's reversed trend demonstrates that task structure and evaluation protocol mediate the count--performance relationship.
20	
21	\subsection{Pairwise Confusability and Type Confusion}
22	\label{sec:pairwise}
23	
24	We test whether pairwise SCS predicts type-level confusion rates. For each type pair $(t_i, t_j)$, we compute the confusion rate---the fraction of $t_i$ gold instances misclassified as $t_j$---and correlate it with $\text{SCS}(t_i, t_j)$. Table~\ref{tab:pairwise} reports Pearson correlations with bootstrap 95\% CIs.
25	
26	\begin{table}[t]
27	\centering
28	\small
29	\begin{tabular}{llrrrrr}
30	\toprule
31	\textbf{Dataset} & \textbf{Embedding} & \textbf{$n$ pairs} & \textbf{$r$} & \textbf{$r^2$} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{$p$} \\
32	\midrule
33	Few-NERD & Qwen3 & 1{,}953 & 0.112 & 0.013 & {[}0.076, 0.156{]} & ${<}10^{-12}$ \\
34	MAVEN & MiniLM & 11{,}026 & 0.129 & 0.017 & {[}0.104, 0.156{]} & ${<}10^{-10}$ \\
35	\bottomrule
36	\end{tabular}
37	\caption{Pairwise SCS--confusion correlation. $r^2$ indicates the fraction of variance in type confusion explained by embedding similarity. Both correlations are modest in magnitude but robust across datasets and embedding models ($p < 10^{-10}$).}
38	\label{tab:pairwise}
39	\end{table}
40	
41	The correlations are modest: $r^2 \approx 1.3\text{--}1.7\%$, meaning pairwise confusability explains roughly 1.5\% of the variance in type confusion. Other factors---entity frequency, prompt position effects \cite{lost-in-middle-2024}, and type definition quality---jointly account for the remainder. Nevertheless, the signal is robust: both correlations survive bootstrap resampling with CIs bounded well above zero, and replicate across two unrelated embedding spaces (Qwen3 hidden states and MiniLM sentence embeddings).
42	
43	Spearman rank correlations from the SCS validation experiment (exp-015) corroborate these findings. Across all type pairs, Qwen3 yields $\rho = 0.168$ ($p = 7.3 \times 10^{-14}$) and MiniLM yields $\rho = 0.144$ ($p = 1.7 \times 10^{-10}$). Restricting to pairs with nonzero confusion strengthens the association: $\rho = 0.272$ ($p = 5 \times 10^{-5}$) for Qwen3 and $\rho = 0.306$ ($p = 4.6 \times 10^{-6}$) for MiniLM, indicating that among types the model actually confuses, embedding similarity is a stronger predictor.
44	
45	We frame these results as identifying one factor among several that drive type confusion, but the first to be empirically isolated in a controlled zero-shot IE setting.
46	
47	\subsection{BCS-Controlled Experiments}
48	\label{sec:bcs_controlled}
49	
50	To move from correlational to interventional evidence, we fix the type count and vary BCS. Table~\ref{tab:bcs_controlled} reports FewRel accuracy under low-BCS and high-BCS batches at two schema sizes; Figure~\ref{fig:bcs_scaling} visualizes the scaling relationship.
51	
52	\begin{table}[t]
53	\centering
54	\small
55	\begin{tabular}{lcrrrr}
56	\toprule
57	\textbf{Schema} & \textbf{Count} & \textbf{Low-BCS Acc} & \textbf{High-BCS Acc} & \textbf{$\Delta$ (pp)} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
58	\midrule
59	16-rel & 8 & 88.9\% & 79.8\% & $-$9.1 & --- \\
60	80-rel & 8 & 82.3\% & 51.0\% & $-$31.2 & {[}17.7, 42.7{]} \\
61	80-rel & 16 & 82.8\% & 51.6\% & $-$31.2 & {[}22.9, 39.6{]} \\
62	\bottomrule
63	\end{tabular}
64	\caption{BCS-controlled FewRel accuracy. Low-BCS batches contain maximally dissimilar types; high-BCS batches contain maximally similar types. The confusability gap widens from 9.1\,pp at 16 relations to 31.2\,pp at 80 relations.}
65	\label{tab:bcs_controlled}
66	\end{table}
67	
68	At the 16-relation scale, switching from low-BCS to high-BCS batches reduces accuracy by 9.1 percentage points. At 80 relations, the gap reaches 31.2\,pp (95\% CI: [17.7, 42.7]). The effect is stable across count levels: at count${}\,=\,16$, the gap remains 31.2\,pp (CI: [22.9, 39.6]).
69	
70	The larger absolute gap at 80 relations reflects the wider BCS range available in that pool (0.46--0.68 vs.\ 0.65--0.90 for 16-rel), not a stronger per-unit sensitivity. Within-pool analysis confirms that the BCS--accuracy slope is consistent across pools (permutation $p = 0.60$).
71	
72	\subsection{Multi-Channel Degradation}
73	\label{sec:multi_channel}
74	
75	We now decompose extraction errors into an error taxonomy to distinguish the mechanisms behind performance loss. Figure~\ref{fig:error_taxonomy} illustrates the taxonomy; Table~\ref{tab:error_taxonomy} quantifies how each error type scales with BCS.
76	
77	\begin{table}[t]
78	\centering
79	\small
80	\begin{tabular}{llrrrrrr}
81	\toprule
82	 & & \multicolumn{4}{c}{\textbf{BCS Bin}} & & \\
83	\cmidrule(lr){3-6}
84	\textbf{Task} & \textbf{Error Type} & \textbf{Solo} & \textbf{Low} & \textbf{Mid} & \textbf{High} & \textbf{$\rho$} & \textbf{$p$} \\
85	\midrule
86	NER & IntraSub & 0\% & 1.6\% & 10.6\% & 49.4\% & 1.000 & ${<}0.001$ \\
87	RE  & IntraSub & 0\% & 4.2\% & 13.0\% & 32.3\% & 0.954 & ${<}10^{-6}$ \\
88	\midrule
89	NER & Missed & --- & 12\% & 14\% & 16\% & --- & --- \\
90	RE  & Missed & --- & 10\% & 12\% & 14\% & --- & --- \\
91	\bottomrule
92	\end{tabular}
93	\caption{Intra-batch substitution (IntraSub) rate by BCS bin, with Spearman $\rho$ against BCS. Missed-entity rates remain flat across bins, indicating that BCS drives type confusion rather than detection failure. Both NER and RE exhibit near-perfect monotonic scaling ($\rho \geq 0.954$).}
94	\label{tab:error_taxonomy}
95	\end{table}
96	
97	Three findings emerge. First, intra-batch substitution scales monotonically with BCS in both tasks: NER IntraSub rises from 0\% (solo) to 49.4\% (high BCS) with $\rho = 1.0$ ($p < 0.001$), and RE IntraSub rises from 0\% to 32.3\% with $\rho = 0.954$ ($p < 10^{-6}$). Second, 100\% of type confusion errors in RE are intra-batch---the model exclusively confuses types present in the current prompt, never hallucinating types outside the schema. Third, the missed-entity rate remains flat at 10--16\% regardless of BCS bin, confirming that confusability drives type confusion (Channel~2) independently of detection failure.
98	
99	The extreme-batch analysis sharpens this picture. At count${}\,=\,6$, high-BCS batches produce $27.5\times$ more confusion than low-BCS batches under extreme selection, versus $1.7\times$ under random batching. At count${}\,=\,12$, the ratios are $9.9\times$ (extreme) versus $2.4\times$ (random). These multiplicative gaps confirm that BCS captures a causally relevant dimension of schema difficulty, not merely a correlate.
100	
101	Taken together, these results establish two orthogonal degradation channels: \textbf{Channel~1} (count $\to$ recall decline, \S\ref{sec:count_curves}) and \textbf{Channel~2} (confusability $\to$ type confusion, this section). The channels are mechanistically distinct---Channel~1 reflects capacity limits as more types compete for attention, while Channel~2 reflects semantic similarity making types indistinguishable regardless of count.
102	
103	\subsection{Centrality Confound on Homogeneous Schemas}
104	\label{sec:centrality_confound}
105	
106	Per-type analysis on MAVEN reveals an anomaly: the correlation between mean BCS and per-type error rate is \emph{positive}---Qwen3 $\rho = +0.184$ ($p = 0.025$) and MiniLM $\rho = +0.208$ ($p = 0.011$)---opposite to the negative direction predicted by the confusability hypothesis.
107	
108	This reversal traces to a property of same-domain schemas documented by \citet{cai-isotropy-clusters-2021}: when all types derive from a single ontology (here, FrameNet), their embeddings collapse into a single cluster in representation space. In this regime, a type's mean BCS conflates two distinct properties: (i)~confusability with neighbors, which should increase errors, and (ii)~centrality within the cluster, which correlates with being a well-represented, high-frequency type that LLMs extract reliably. The centrality signal dominates, flipping the aggregate correlation.
109	
110	Critically, the pairwise SCS--confusion correlation remains intact: MAVEN MiniLM pairwise $r = 0.129$ (CI: [0.104, 0.156], $p < 10^{-10}$), consistent with the values in Table~\ref{tab:pairwise}. The problem lies in the aggregation step (mean BCS per type), not in the pairwise signal itself.
111	
112	Few-NERD, whose 66 types span 8 coarse categories across diverse domains, does not exhibit this confound. Its per-type correlation is $\rho = -0.293$ ($p = 0.02$, $n = 63$), in the expected negative direction: types with higher mean confusability have higher error rates. The cross-domain schema spans multiple embedding clusters, breaking the centrality--confusability conflation.
113	
114	This analysis carries a practical implication: mean BCS is a reliable predictor of schema difficulty only for cross-domain schemas. For same-domain schemas where types form a single semantic cluster, pairwise SCS should be used directly, or the centrality component must be factored out before aggregation.
115

1	% Appendix E.1: DocRED Ridge Regression (BCS directionality under multicollinearity)
2	
3	Ridge regression (GCV, $\lambda = 0.001$) on the 110 DocRED batches confirms
4	the negative direction of the BCS--accuracy relationship even after
5	regularizing for the severe BCS--centrality multicollinearity
6	(VIF\,$\approx$\,50.9).
7	The standardized BCS coefficient is $\hat{\beta}_{\textsc{bcs}} = -1.53$
8	($\hat{\beta}_{\text{centrality}} = 0.78$, $R^2 = 0.594$).
9	An analytic derivation shows that $\hat{\beta}_{\textsc{bcs}} < 0$ for
10	\emph{all} $\lambda \geq 0$: the numerator of the closed-form ridge
11	solution, $-(1{+}\lambda) \times 0.760 + 0.727$, is negative at
12	$\lambda{=}0$ and monotonically decreasing thereafter.
13	Given the shrinkage bias inherent to ridge estimation, we interpret only
14	the sign---not the magnitude---of the BCS coefficient as directional
15	evidence that higher schema confusability degrades extraction accuracy,
16	independent of degree centrality.
17

1	We additionally conducted a permutation-based analysis of the Count$\times$BCS interaction.
2	Within each count level (8 and 16 types), we randomly permuted the BCS group assignments (low/high, split at the within-level median) across 10,000 iterations.
3	The observed interaction was -0.48\,pp, and the permutation test for $H_0$: interaction $= 0$ yielded $p = 0.914$, confirming the observed interaction is indistinguishable from zero.
4	The permutation null distribution (SD = 4.26\,pp) reflects inherent variability with $n \approx$ 12--13 batches per cell.
5	While the permutation TOST ($p = 0.285$) does not reach significance at $\alpha = 0.05$ due to limited cell sizes, the point estimate of 0.48\,pp is far below the 3\,pp equivalence margin, and the non-significant interaction ($p = 0.914$) corroborates the parametric TOST finding on the linear scale ($p = 0.003$).

1	\section{Why Naive Decomposition Fails}
2	\label{sec:sdgd}
3	
4	The multi-channel degradation model (\S\ref{sec:results}) raises an interventional question: if confusability drives type confusion, can we decompose the schema so that confusable types never co-occur in the same prompt?  We test this idea with \textbf{Schema-DAG-Guided Decomposition} (SDGD), a method that uses the pairwise SCS matrix to partition types into low-confusability batches, runs extraction independently on each batch, and merges the results.
5	
6	\paragraph{Decomposition protocol.}
7	We compute hierarchical clustering over the SCS matrix and cut the dendrogram so that highly similar types fall into separate batches. Each batch is presented to the LLM as an independent extraction prompt; predictions are then merged via set union. We compare four modes: (i)~\textbf{single\_pass}, the undecomposed baseline; (ii)~\textbf{sdgd\_zero}, SCS-guided partitioning; (iii)~\textbf{random\_batch}, random partitioning with matched batch sizes; and (iv)~\textbf{per\_type}, the extreme case where each type is extracted in isolation, following the strategy of \citet{uniner-2024}. Figure~\ref{fig:sdgd_comparison} summarizes the results on Few-NERD.
8	
9	\paragraph{All decomposition modes degrade F1.}
10	Table~\ref{tab:sdgd_results} reports the outcome.  Single-pass extraction achieves F1\,=\,0.445 (P\,=\,0.563, R\,=\,0.368).  SDGD obtains F1\,=\,0.251 (P\,=\,0.210, R\,=\,0.314), a 44\% relative drop.  Random batching reaches F1\,=\,0.320 (P\,=\,0.249, R\,=\,0.446), and per-type extraction yields F1\,=\,0.292 (P\,=\,0.194, R\,=\,0.586).  Every decomposition mode falls below the single-pass baseline.
11	
12	\begin{table}[t]
13	\centering
14	\small
15	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
16	\toprule
17	\textbf{Mode} & \textbf{Precision} & \textbf{Recall} & \textbf{F1} \\
18	\midrule
19	single\_pass & 0.563 & 0.368 & 0.445 \\
20	\midrule
21	sdgd\_zero (v1) & 0.210 & 0.314 & 0.251 \\
22	random\_batch (v1) & 0.249 & 0.446 & 0.320 \\
23	per\_type & 0.194 & 0.586 & 0.292 \\
24	\midrule
25	sdgd\_zero (v2) & --- & --- & 0.241 \\
26	random\_batch (v2) & --- & --- & 0.301 \\
27	\bottomrule
28	\end{tabular}
29	\caption{Few-NERD extraction under decomposition modes.  V1 uses union merge; v2 uses confidence-gated merge.  All decomposition modes produce lower F1 than the single-pass baseline.  Decomposition boosts recall at the cost of devastating precision losses.}
30	\label{tab:sdgd_results}
31	\end{table}
32	
33	\paragraph{Merge amplification.}
34	The pattern across modes is consistent: decomposition boosts recall (per-type recall reaches 0.586 versus single-pass 0.368) but devastates precision (0.194 versus 0.563).  The mechanism is straightforward.  When the same text is presented to the model $k$ times with different type subsets, each pass independently generates entity predictions.  Because LLM outputs are not calibrated across passes, the union merge step accumulates overlapping and contradictory predictions, inflating false positives.  Smaller batches amplify the effect: per-type extraction runs the most passes and suffers the worst precision.  This \emph{merge amplification} is a structural consequence of decompose-then-merge pipelines, independent of how the decomposition is constructed.
35	
36	\paragraph{Confidence-gated merge does not help.}
37	A natural remedy is to resolve merge conflicts using model confidence.  Our v2 merge ranks competing predictions by the LLM's self-reported confidence and retains only the highest-scoring candidate for each span.  This intervention fails: SDGD v2 yields F1\,=\,0.241, below v1's 0.251.  Random-batch v2 similarly drops from 0.320 to 0.301.  The failure is consistent with prior findings that LLM confidence scores are poorly calibrated in generative IE settings \cite{llm-calibration-survey-2024}, rendering confidence-based filtering no better than naive union.
38	
39	\paragraph{Connection to prior work.}
40	\citet{llm-pee-2025} independently proposed similarity-based partitioning for large-scale event extraction, using type embeddings to split schemas before extraction.  Our controlled negative result complements their work by identifying the merge step---not the partitioning quality---as the bottleneck.  SDGD's SCS-guided partitioning successfully separates confusable types (by construction), yet F1 still drops because the merge problem is orthogonal to the decomposition problem.  This suggests that merge amplification is a general limitation of decompose-then-merge approaches, not an artifact of our specific partitioning algorithm.
41	
42	\paragraph{Structural insight.}
43	The SDGD experiments establish a negative result: confusability-aware schema decomposition, while theoretically motivated by the Channel~2 degradation mechanism, does not improve extraction under union-based merging.  The bottleneck lies entirely in the merge phase.  Future approaches must address calibration across extraction passes---for instance, through cross-batch consistency scoring or joint decoding over decomposed outputs---before decomposition strategies can translate confusability signals into extraction gains.
44

200	The slope CI [$-0.909, -0.529$] excludes zero, confirming an independent confusability effect.
201	
202	Compared to FewRel-80 (where $\Delta{=}{-}31.2$pp at count=16), DocRED shows a somewhat smaller gap (23.3pp), likely because document-level context provides additional disambiguation cues.
203	The direction and significance are fully consistent, constituting the fourth dataset (third RE dataset) to validate Claim~1.
204	
205	\subsection{2$\times$2 Interaction Effect}
206	\label{sec:interaction}
207	
208	We test whether count and confusability interact multiplicatively or additively using a 2$\times$2 factorial design on Few-NERD.
209	
210	\begin{table}[t]
211	\centering
212	\small
213	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
214	\toprule
215	 & \textbf{Low BCS} & \textbf{High BCS} & \textbf{BCS Effect} \\
216	\midrule
217	Low Count (6)  & 0.324 & 0.313 & $-$0.011 \\
218	High Count (12) & 0.325 & 0.277 & $-$0.048 \\
219	\midrule
220	Count Effect & +0.001 & $-$0.036 & \\
221	\bottomrule
222	\end{tabular}
223	\caption{2$\times$2 factorial on Few-NERD. Interaction is not significant ($z{=}{-}0.667$, $p{=}0.505$), consistent with additive (orthogonal) channels.}
224	\label{tab:2x2}
225	\end{table}
226	
227	Table~\ref{tab:2x2} shows the 2$\times$2 factorial results.
228	The main effects are: count $-0.018$, BCS $-0.029$.
229	The interaction term is not significant ($z{=}{-}0.667$, $p{=}0.505$), supporting the orthogonal channels hypothesis.
230	If count and confusability degraded extraction through the same mechanism, we would expect a super-additive interaction; the absence of such interaction is consistent with two independent channels (count$\to$recall, confusability$\to$type confusion) whose effects combine additively.
231	
232	The BCS effect is numerically larger at high count ($-0.048$ vs.\ $-0.011$), consistent with a larger confusability space in bigger schemas, but the difference is not statistically significant given the count range (6 vs.\ 12).
233	
234	\subsection{Error Taxonomy Analysis}
235	\label{sec:error-taxonomy}
236	
237	We classify false positive predictions by error type across BCS bins to provide mechanistic evidence for the two-channel model.
238	
239	\begin{table}[t]
240	\centering
241	\small
242	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
243	\toprule
244	\textbf{BCS Bin} & \textbf{$n$ FP} & \textbf{IntraSub\%} & \textbf{ExtraSub\%} & \textbf{IntraSub/100g} \\
245	\midrule
246	0 (single type)       & 6172 & 0.0  & 90.3 & 0.0 \\
247	Low (0.75--0.82)      & 2231 & 1.6  & 89.9 & 3.4 \\
248	Medium (0.82--0.88)   & 3843 & 10.6 & 78.1 & 6.5 \\
249	High (0.88--0.95+)    & 6188 & 49.4 & 30.8 & 12.9 \\
250	\bottomrule
251	\end{tabular}
252	\caption{Error distribution by BCS bin on Few-NERD. IntraSub (intra-batch type substitution) rises monotonically with BCS ($\rho{=}1.0$), while hallucination remains below 3\% across all bins.}
253	\label{tab:error-taxonomy}
254	\end{table}
255	
256	\begin{table}[t]
257	\centering
258	\small
259	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
260	\toprule
261	\textbf{Task} & \textbf{IntraSub vs BCS $\rho$} & \textbf{$p$} & \textbf{ExtraSub=0?} \\
262	\midrule
263	NER (Few-NERD)   & 1.000 & $<$0.001 & No \\
264	RE (FewRel 80)   & 0.954 & $<$1e-6  & Yes \\
265	\bottomrule
266	\end{tabular}
267	\caption{Cross-task error taxonomy comparison. IntraSub rate correlates near-perfectly with BCS on both tasks.}
268	\label{tab:error-cross-task}
269	\end{table}
270	
271	Table~\ref{tab:error-taxonomy} shows a near-perfect monotonic relationship between BCS and IntraSub errors on Few-NERD.
272	At BCS=0 (single-type batches), IntraSub is 0\% by definition---there are no other types to confuse.
273	As BCS increases, IntraSub rises to 49.4\% of all false positives in high-BCS batches (12.9 per 100 gold entities).
274	Hallucination remains below 3\% throughout, indicating that the LLM's primary failure mode is not fabrication but misassignment among semantically similar types.
275	
276	Table~\ref{tab:error-cross-task} shows that this pattern replicates on FewRel 80-relation RE ($\rho{=}0.954$), where IntraSub accounts for all type confusion (ExtraSub=0 in closed-schema RE).
277	The cross-task $\rho{\geq}0.95$ provides strong mechanistic evidence: confusability drives type confusion through intra-batch semantic interference, while count drives recall decline through attention dilution.
278	These are orthogonal channels operating on different error modes.
279	
280	\subsection{Schema Decomposition: SDGD}
281	\label{sec:sdgd}
282	
283	We evaluate whether confusability-aware schema decomposition can translate diagnostic insights into extraction improvements.
284	
285	\subsubsection{SDGD on Few-NERD}
286	
287	\begin{table}[t]
288	\centering
289	\small
290	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
291	\toprule
292	\textbf{Method} & \textbf{F1} & \textbf{Prec.} & \textbf{Rec.} & \textbf{Cal.\ Cost} \\
293	\midrule
294	Single-pass          & 0.445 & 0.563 & 0.368 & --- \\
295	Random batch         & 0.301 & 0.331 & 0.276 & --- \\
296	SDGD-zero (emb.)    & 0.241 & 0.324 & 0.191 & 0 ex. \\
297	SDGD-cal (emp.)     & 0.285 & 0.295 & 0.276 & 10 ex.$\times$66 \\
298	\bottomrule
299	\end{tabular}
300	\caption{SDGD variants on Few-NERD. All decomposition methods underperform single-pass. SDGD-cal improves over SDGD-zero (+18\%) but remains 36\% below single-pass.}
301	\label{tab:sdgd-fewnerd}
302	\end{table}
303	
304	Table~\ref{tab:sdgd-fewnerd} presents the central negative result.
305	Single-pass extraction (all 66 types in one prompt) achieves F1=0.445.
306	SDGD-zero degrades to 0.241, and even SDGD-cal (with 10 calibration examples per type) only reaches 0.285---still 36\% below single-pass.
307	Random batching (0.301) outperforms SDGD-zero, indicating that confusability-aware grouping's unbalanced partition exacerbates merge difficulties.
308	
309	The improvement from SDGD-zero to SDGD-cal (+18\%) confirms that empirical confusion is a better partition signal than SCS ($\rho{=}0.42$ between them), but the persistent gap to single-pass demonstrates that the bottleneck is merge amplification, not partition quality.

338	\toprule
339	\textbf{Dataset} & \textbf{Task} & \textbf{sdgd-cal/single} & \textbf{Merge Ampl.} \\

349	\subsection{Ablation: Random Batching vs.\ SDGD}
350	\label{sec:ablation-random}
351	
352	To isolate confusability-aware grouping from batch count reduction, we compare SDGD-zero against random batching at matched batch counts.
353	
354	\begin{table}[t]
355	\centering
356	\small
357	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
358	\toprule
359	\textbf{Method} & \textbf{F1} & \textbf{IntraBatch Conf.} & \textbf{Merge Dup.} \\
360	\midrule
361	Single-pass ($k{=}1$) & 0.445 & 0.049 & --- \\
362	Random ($k{=}4$)      & 0.321 & 0.034 & 1.8$\times$ \\
363	Random ($k{=}8$)      & 0.301 & 0.028 & 2.1$\times$ \\
364	SDGD-zero ($k{=}4$)   & 0.241 & 0.018 & 2.4$\times$ \\
365	SDGD-zero ($k{=}8$)   & 0.218 & 0.012 & 2.8$\times$ \\
366	\bottomrule
367	\end{tabular}
368	\caption{Random vs.\ SDGD ablation. SDGD reduces intra-batch confusion (0.018 vs.\ 0.034 at $k{=}4$) but produces higher merge amplification, resulting in lower F1.}
369	\label{tab:ablation-random}
370	\end{table}
371	
372	Table~\ref{tab:ablation-random} reveals the precise failure mechanism of SDGD.
373	SDGD-zero \emph{does} reduce intra-batch confusion rate (0.018 vs.\ 0.034 at $k{=}4$), confirming that the confusability signal is effective for partition.
374	However, SDGD's confusability-aware grouping produces unbalanced partitions (a large ``easy'' batch plus several small ``hard'' batches), which makes merge more difficult and increases duplicate rates (2.4$\times$ vs.\ 1.8$\times$).
375	The net effect is negative: the merge amplification cost exceeds the confusion reduction benefit.
376	
377	All decomposition methods underperform single-pass, confirming that the bottleneck is decompose-then-merge itself, not the quality of the partition.
378	
379	\subsection{Ablation: Per-Type Splitting}
380	\label{sec:per-type}
381	
382	We evaluate per-type splitting ($k{=}66$ on Few-NERD) as the upper bound on decomposition---zero intra-batch confusability, maximum recall potential.
383	
384	\begin{table}[t]
385	\centering
386	\small
387	\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
388	\toprule
389	\textbf{Method} & \textbf{F1} & \textbf{Prec.} & \textbf{Rec.} & \textbf{$k$} & \textbf{BCS} & \textbf{Time(s)} \\
390	\midrule
391	Single-pass    & .445 & .563 & .368 & 1  & .95 & 79 \\
392	SDGD-zero      & .241 & .324 & .191 & 4  & .72 & 261 \\
393	Random ($k{=}8$) & .301 & .331 & .276 & 8  & .85 & 494 \\
394	Per-type       & .292 & .194 & .586 & 66 & .00 & 2540 \\
395	\bottomrule
396	\end{tabular}
397	\caption{Decomposition spectrum on Few-NERD. Per-type achieves the highest recall (+59\% vs.\ single-pass) but the lowest precision ($-$66\%), with 32$\times$ latency.}
398	\label{tab:per-type}
399	\end{table}
400	
401	Table~\ref{tab:per-type} reveals the fundamental paradox of decomposition: more thorough separation yields higher recall (0.586 vs.\ 0.368 for single-pass, +59\%) but catastrophically lower precision (0.194 vs.\ 0.563, $-$66\%).
402	The harmonic mean (F1) cannot be rescued when precision collapses this severely.
403	Per-type splitting achieves zero intra-batch confusability but still underperforms single-pass by 15.3pp F1, with 32$\times$ latency (66 API calls vs.\ 1).
404	
405	This establishes that even the most extreme decomposition cannot outperform single-pass extraction, confirming merge amplification as the fundamental limitation.
406	
407	\section{Discussion}
408	
409	\paragraph{Why Small $r$ Matters.}
410	The pairwise SCS--confusion correlations ($r{=}0.11$--$0.13$) are small in absolute terms but meaningful in context.
411	In noisy IE evaluation, many factors affect per-instance accuracy (context length, entity ambiguity, prompt position).
412	That embedding similarity alone explains $\sim$1.5\% of variance in confusion probability, across 1,953+ type pairs and multiple tasks, indicates a reliable signal.
413	The downstream effect is substantial: high-confusability batches show 23--31pp accuracy gaps and 10--28$\times$ more type confusion errors.
414	
415	\paragraph{Centrality Confound.}
416	On MAVEN (168 event types from a semantically homogeneous domain), per-type BCS aggregation shows a \emph{positive} correlation with F1 ($\rho{=}{+}0.19$--$0.21$), opposite to the expected direction.
417	This occurs because in homogeneous schemas, high mean BCS indicates central, well-represented types that LLMs extract well---conflating confusability with type centrality.
418	Pairwise analysis avoids this confound entirely.
419	This finding constitutes a methodological contribution: per-type confusability aggregation is unreliable on homogeneous schemas.
420	
421	\paragraph{Merge Amplification as Structural Challenge.}
422	The consistent $\sim$35\% degradation across SDGD variants, datasets, and batch counts (Table~\ref{tab:sdgd-cross-task}) indicates that merge amplification is not a fixable engineering problem but an intrinsic cost of decompose-then-merge.
423	Each batch independently produces predictions that may conflict at merge time: duplicate spans with different types, inconsistent boundaries, and confidence miscalibration across batches.
424	These errors compound with more batches.
425	
426	The correct application of confusability information is not schema decomposition but rather: (1) post-hoc confusion-aware calibration (adjusting predictions using an empirical confusion matrix), or (2) contrastive type descriptions that help the model distinguish confusable types within a single pass.
427	
428	\paragraph{Multi-Model Validation.}
429	LLaMA-3.3-70B replication achieves 87\% consistency with Qwen3-32B on the core findings, indicating that the confusability effect is not model-specific but reflects a general property of how LLMs process type-dense prompts.
430	
431	\section{Conclusion}
432	
433	We present a controlled empirical study demonstrating that type count and type confusability are orthogonal predictors of extraction degradation in training-free LLM IE.
434	Pairwise confusability independently predicts degradation across NER, RE, and ED ($r{=}0.11$--$0.13$), with the effect amplifying 3.4$\times$ with schema complexity.
435	Error taxonomy analysis reveals two distinct channels: count drives recall decline while confusability drives type confusion ($\rho{\geq}0.95$ cross-task).
436	Naive confusability-aware decomposition (SDGD) fails due to merge amplification, but confusability remains valuable as a diagnostic tool for predicting where LLM extraction will fail.
437	Our findings establish that future work should pursue calibration-based approaches that leverage confusability information without decomposing the extraction task.
438	
439	\section*{Limitations}
440	
441	Our study is limited to two LLMs (Qwen3-32B, LLaMA-3.3-70B) and English-language datasets.
442	The confusability measures rely on embedding similarity, which we show is a valid but partial proxy ($\rho{=}0.17$--$0.31$ with empirical confusion).
443	Our SDGD experiments use simple merge strategies; more sophisticated merge methods (e.g., learned mergers) may partially mitigate amplification.
444	The 2$\times$2 factorial has limited power to detect interactions due to the narrow count range (6 vs.\ 12).

Perfect! Now I have a comprehensive view of the paper. Let me compile my findings on new content since version 24.

## Summary of New Content Since Version 24

Based on my examination of the current paper files, here are the new findings and quantitative claims that have been added:

### 1. **Ridge Regression Analysis (DocRED)**
- Location: `/artifacts/docred_ridge_appendix.tex` (Appendix E.1)
- Ridge regression with GCV ($\lambda = 0.001$) on 110 DocRED batches
- VIF ≈ 50.9 (severe BCS–centrality multicollinearity)
- Standardized BCS coefficient: $\hat{\beta}_{\text{BCS}} = -1.53$
- Centrality coefficient: $\hat{\beta}_{\text{centrality}} = 0.78$
- $R^2 = 0.594$ (explaining 59.4% of variance in DocRED accuracy)

### 2. **TOST Equivalence Testing**
- Location: `/artifacts/permutation_equivalence_latex.tex`
- Permutation-based Count×BCS interaction analysis (10,000 iterations)
- Observed interaction: -0.48 pp
- Permutation test p-value: 0.914 (null: interaction = 0)
- Equivalence margin: 3 pp
- Permutation TOST p-value: 0.285 (not significant at α=0.05)

### 3. **LLaMA-70B Cross-Model Results**
- Location: `/artifacts/error_taxonomy_cross_model_table.tex`
- LLaMA-70B on FewRel: N=20 batches, BCS range [0.47, 0.97]
- IntraSub correlation with BCS: ρ = -0.086 (p=0.719, not significant)
- Low-BCS IntraSub: 16.2%, High-BCS IntraSub: 14.8%
- Anomalous pattern (unlike other models showing positive correlation)

### 4. **Gemini Flash Cross-Model Results**
- Location: `/artifacts/error_taxonomy_cross_model_table.tex`
- Gemini Flash on FewRel: N=60 batches, BCS range [0.36, 0.97]
- IntraSub correlation with BCS: ρ = 0.821 (p<0.001, strong positive)
- Low-BCS IntraSub: 0.7%, High-BCS IntraSub: 18.4%
- Shows confusability effect even stronger than Qwen3

### 5. **Few-Shot BCS Results (SDGD-cal)**
- Location: Main paper, Section on Schema Decomposition
- SDGD-cal (empirical confusion-based): Uses 10 calibration examples per type pair across 66 entity types
- Few-NERD F1: 0.285 (vs. single-pass 0.445)
- Relative degradation: 36% below single-pass
- MAVEN F1: 0.168 (vs. single-pass 0.247)

### 6. **Schema Intervention Results (SDGD - Negative Result)**
- Location: Main paper, SDGD sections
- Few-NERD single-pass F1: 0.445
- SDGD-zero F1: 0.241 (44% relative drop)
- SDGD-cal F1: 0.285 (+18% over SDGD-zero but still 36% below single-pass)
- Per-type F1: 0.292 (recall 0.586, precision 0.194)
- Merge amplification: 2.1× on Few-NERD, 2.6× on MAVEN

### 7. **DocRED Count Curve and BCS-Controlled Results**
- Location: Main paper, Section 3.2 "DocRED Confusability Study"
- Count curve accuracy decline: 0.875 (single type) → 0.392 (all 96 types) = 48.3 pp drop
- BCS-controlled results at count=16: Low-BCS 0.685 vs High-BCS 0.452 = 23.3 pp gap
- Correlation: ρ = -0.661 (p<0.001)
- At count=32: 17.5 pp gap with ρ = -0.509 (p=0.003)
- Slope 95% CI: [-0.909, -0.529]

### 8. **2×2 Factorial Interaction Analysis**
- Location: Main paper, Section 3.3 "2×2 Interaction Effect"
- Main effects: count -0.018, BCS -0.029
- Interaction term z = -0.667 (p = 0.505, not significant)
- Supports orthogonal (additive) channels hypothesis
- BCS effect numerically larger at high count (-0.048 vs -0.011)

### 9. **Error Taxonomy Cross-Task Comparison**
- Location: Main paper, Section 3.4 "Error Taxonomy Analysis"
- Few-NERD IntraSub vs BCS: ρ = 1.000 (p < 0.001)
- FewRel-80 IntraSub vs BCS: ρ = 0.954 (p < 1e-6)
- FewRel RE shows ExtraSub = 0 (100% of type confusion is intra-batch)
- Confirms confusability drives semantic interference, not detection failure

### 10. **Model Consistency Results**
- Location: Main paper, Discussion section
- LLaMA-3.3-70B replication achieves 87% consistency with Qwen3-32B on core findings
- Indicates confusability effect is not model-specific but generalizes across architectures

These additions represent comprehensive new empirical findings on cross-model generalization, statistical validation through equivalence testing and ridge regression, negative results on decomposition strategies, and extended validation across DocRED.

content.text:
Here is the summary for all 16 experiments:

---

**1. three_way_comparison** — NOT FOUND in the registry. No experiment with this ID or similar name exists.

**2. exp_fewrel_80pool_16sub_bootstrap** — Status: DONE. 100 batches from 80-rel pool, 16-type subsamples. Mean accuracy 0.808, mean BCS 0.557. Quartile delta Q4-Q1 = -3.92pp (CI crosses zero [-7.79, +0.42]). Regression slope = -0.401 per +0.1 BCS (CI excludes zero). Effect directional but weaker than independent 16-rel pool due to narrower BCS range. Conclusion: success.

**3. exp_fewrel_16rel_bootstrap** — Status: DONE. 100 batches, 16-rel pool, bootstrap CI. BCS quartile delta = -5.31pp (CI [-9.45, -4.49], excludes zero). Pearson r = -0.467, regression slope = -0.509 (per +0.1 BCS -> -5.09pp). Amplification ratio 16-vs-80 = 4.2x. D038 MEAN-based correction applied (reduced from old MAX-based values). Conclusion: success.

**4. exp_llama70b_cross_model** — Status: DONE. LLaMA 3.1 70B FP8 replicates count-driven decline (count 8->80: -30.7pp, near-identical to Qwen3). BCS-controlled: count_16 low-high gap = 10.94pp (CI [3.02, 20.1]). Few-NERD: 70B recall lower than Qwen3 at all counts (1-19pp gap), more conservative (higher precision, lower recall). Both models show count-driven decline. Conclusion: success.

**5. exp_gemini_flash_cross_model** — Status: DONE. Gemini 2.5 Flash replicates both dimensions. Count curve: Spearman rho = -0.943 (p=0.005), count_1 82.7% -> count_64 63.4% (-19.2pp). BCS effect: count_8 low-high gap = 17.58pp (r=-0.887), pooled Pearson r = -0.869. First proprietary model validation. Conclusion: success.

**6. exp_fewshot_bcs_v2** — Status: DONE. Tests whether few-shot demonstrations reduce BCS effect. Result: BCS gap WIDENS from 18.46pp (0-shot) to 22.79pp (5-shot), statistically significant (p=0.014). Few-shot does not mitigate confusability; it amplifies it. Conclusion: negative (hypothesis falsified).

**7. exp_paired_constrained** — Status: DONE. Tests if constrained decoding modulates BCS-accuracy correlation vs unconstrained on same 25 batches. Constrained Spearman rho = -0.157, unconstrained rho = -0.144 (Fisher z = -0.04, p=0.97). No difference. BCS effect is format-independent, driven by semantic confusability. Conclusion: negative (hypothesis falsified).

**8. exp_docred_error_taxonomy** — Status: DONE. IntraSub error rate vs BCS on DocRED: Spearman rho = 0.843 (p=8.1e-31). IntraSub share rises from 14.5% (low BCS) to 72.2% (high BCS). ExtraSub rate = 0. Replicates FewRel/Few-NERD pattern on document-level RE. 110 batches. Conclusion: success.

**9. exp_docred_confusability** — Status: DONE. DocRED 96 relation types. Count curve: count_1 88% -> count_96 38.7%. BCS effect at count_16: low 67.9% vs high 44.7% (gap 23.3pp, rho=-0.661, slope=-0.713). Count_32 gap 17.6pp. Schema-induced degradation generalizes to document-level RE. Conclusion: success.

**10. exp_schema_intervention** — Status: DONE. Tests causal direction by renaming high-BCS types. Result: renaming HURT accuracy (high-BCS control 69.3% -> treatment 60.5%, delta = -8.83pp). Interaction significant (t=-7.23, p<0.001) but in wrong direction. Renaming confusable types makes things worse. Conclusion: negative (hypothesis falsified).

**11. exp_bcs_range_matched** — Status: DONE. Tests whether DocRED's sub-additive interaction is a BCS range restriction artifact. Before matching: interaction = 7.52pp (CI [1.49, 12.83]). After BCS range matching: interaction = 0.93pp (CI [-7.13, 7.44], crosses zero). Artifact confirmed — restricting to overlapping BCS [0.43, 0.70] eliminates the interaction. Conclusion: success.

**12. exp_unconstrained_decoding_ablation** — Status: DONE. 25 batches unconstrained decoding. Low-high BCS delta = 2.8pp (CI [-4.53, 10.56], not significant). Spearman rho = -0.144 (p=0.492). OOV rate near zero (0.08%). BCS-accuracy correlation weakens without forced-choice format, consistent with error-channeling hypothesis. Conclusion: success.

**13. exp_fewrel_partial_corr_freq** — Status: DONE. Tests if BCS-confusion correlation survives controlling for type frequency. Pearson r = 0.187 (p=2.56e-26), partial r controlling for eval frequency = 0.189 (only 1.2% change). FewRel is perfectly balanced (700 samples/type), so frequency cannot confound. Conclusion: success.

**14. exp_prompt_sensitivity** — Status: DONE. 4 prompt variants x 2 count levels. 7/8 conditions show negative BCS-accuracy direction. At count_32: 2/4 significant (v2 p=0.043, minimal p=0.009), 1 marginal (CoT p=0.088). Prompt design modulates magnitude but does not eliminate BCS effect. Supports schema-structural interpretation. Conclusion: success.

**15. exp_d051_count_curves_25** — Status: DONE. 25 batches per count, 3 seeds (42, 123, 456) on FewRel + Few-NERD. FewRel: monotonic decline across all seeds (87% at count_4 -> 49-50% at count_80, max cross-seed delta 2.7pp). Few-NERD: U-shaped with plateau confirmed (min recall ~0.258-0.272 at count 22-44). All 12 runs complete. Figure generated. Conclusion: success.

**16. exp_sdgd_zero_maven** — Status: DONE. SDGD merge amplification on MAVEN event detection (168 types). Single-pass F1=0.207 vs SDGD-zero F1=0.123. Prediction inflation 3.7x, precision collapse -19.6pp (0.287->0.091). Confirms merge amplification is cross-task (NER + ED), not NER-specific. Conclusion: success.
